architecture.mechanism: Accelerated corrosion-fatigue testing at elevated temperatures using a temperature-accelerated S-N and crack growth calibration methodology to predict long-term seawater fatigue damage in offshore wind steel structures.
architecture.intervention: Apply the paper's temperature-accelerated corrosion-fatigue S-N and crack growth equations during materials qualification of the monopile steel and any applied coating system, using elevated-temperature seawater immersion tests to calibrate in-service fatigue life and to identify a coating or surface-treatment threshold (e.g., a cathodic-protection-free barrier coating) that prevents the crack-growth acceleration seen in seawater, so that no sacrificial anodes and no diver inspection are required.
architecture.expected_effect: Quantified reduction of corrosion-fatigue crack initiation and growth rates on the monopile steel in the North Sea splash and submerged zones, extending structural life toward the 20-25 year design envelope and eliminating the need for sacrificial anode retrofit and subsea inspection, with total protection cost kept under 50,000 USD per foundation per decade.
architecture.falsification_test: Manufacture replicate monopile steel coupons with and without the candidate coating, run paired fatigue tests at the paper's elevated temperature in a salt-spray/seawater environment per its two calibration equations, and compare the S-N curves and crack-growth rates; if the coated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in seawater-accelerated fatigue damage relative to uncoated controls at equivalent accelerated exposure, the intervention fails.
